content: 1. Over-fertilization of small lakes and reservoirs can lead to significant ecological imbalances, as noted by Conover and Chasko in 1985. 2. Guideline values for water quality are primarily aimed at protecting public health. However, no specific guideline values have been established for aesthetic and nuisance aspects of water bodies. 3. Operational monitoring of aesthetic aspects often involves debris surveys. Bartram and Rees (2000) discuss methods for conducting such surveys, which can provide information on the types, quantities, and distribution of debris, identify sources of debris, assess the effectiveness of legislation and coastal management policies, and explore public health issues related to debris. 4. In the Catalunya region of Spain, a monitoring program evaluates both microbial water quality and aesthetic aspects of water and sand. Microbial water quality is assessed weekly, while aesthetic aspects are evaluated up to five times a week. Data collected include the presence and amount of plastics, sanitary residues, algae, tar, oil, litter, abnormal water color, and other visually displeasing elements. 5. The aesthetic data are combined with microbial water quality data to produce a comprehensive grading for beaches. Poor aesthetic conditions can downgrade an excellent microbial grading to a lower overall grade. 6. Weekly reports on beach conditions are shared with municipalities, tourist offices, NGOs, and media outlets. Municipalities also receive detailed reports with raw microbial data, visual inspection results, and recommendations for improvements. 7. Marine debris monitoring is well-established, with initiatives like the OSPAR Convention monitoring 50 indicator beaches in the North-East Atlantic since 1998. However, such activities are costly. 8. International programs like the Blue Flag certification include litter management as part of their criteria. Beach litter surveys are also examples of citizen science projects, as seen in the UK’s Marine Conservation Society’s decade-long beach litter data collection. 9. Argentina incorporated aesthetic and nuisance aspects into its 2017 environmental health guidelines. 10. Operational monitoring for nuisance aspects may include observations and measurements to assess conditions that promote nuisance levels of insects, jellyfish, and non-native animals, as well as the effectiveness of control measures. 11. Beach cleaning, whether mechanical or manual, can remove litter and algal wrack. Mechanical cleaning involves motorized equipment with sieves to filter litter from sand but may not capture smaller items like cigarette butts. Manual cleaning is recommended for reducing ecological impacts. 12. Excessive macroalgae, such as Ulva, can indicate nutrient pollution. Addressing the pollution source can improve conditions. Recommendations include leaving natural wrack on less-used beaches, relocating wrack to unused areas, and replacing mechanical cleaning with manual methods. 13. Smoking bans on beaches, first implemented in Hawaii in 1993, have been successful in reducing litter and are now adopted in various countries. Portable ashtrays have also been trialed as an alternative. 14. For beaches allowing dogs, proper disposal of dog waste is encouraged through the provision of bins and waste bags. Dog bans or zoning may be implemented during bathing seasons. 15. Volunteer beach clean-ups have grown significantly, with international initiatives involving over a million participants in 122 countries by 2018. 16. Insect management on beaches depends on the species. Preventive measures include wearing protective clothing, using insect repellents, and maintaining good sanitation to eliminate breeding sites. 17. Mosquito control involves surveillance, larval treatments, and avoiding standing water. Biting midges can be deterred with outdoor fans and UV light traps. Sandflies are best managed by avoiding the beach during peak activity times and using insect repellents. 18. Jellyfish stings can be prevented by avoiding contact, wearing protective clothing, and adhering to warnings. Proper first aid includes removing nematocysts, rinsing with vinegar, and applying heat or local anesthetics. Severe stings require medical attention. 19. Solid waste management and discouraging bird feeding can reduce nuisance bird species. Proper waste disposal and covered bins are essential. 20. The My Beach, Your Beach initiative in Scotland aimed to change behaviors related to littering, dog fouling, and gull feeding. It achieved a 12–15% reduction in litter and increased public awareness. 21. Transparent water and litter-free beaches with minimal nuisances are vital for promoting the health of coastal communities and ecosystems. Global strategies are needed to address large-scale issues like excessive macroalgae, jellyfish, and offshore litter.
